   517	        fixedBinTrace P.model (a * pauliRZBlock z) = β)
   518	
   519	/-- The Pauli win predicate, with constructor-shape rejection.  This is
   520	`def:pauli-win-predicate` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`,
   521	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1126-1225`.
   522	-/
   523	noncomputable def pauliWinPredicate (P : AdmissibleParams) :
   524	    PauliQuestion P → PauliQuestion P → PauliAnswer P → PauliAnswer P → Bool :=
   525	  open Classical in
   526	  fun (tA, xA) (tB, xB) a b =>
   527	    if validPauliAnswer tA a && validPauliAnswer tB b then
   528	      if tA = tB then
   529	        decide (a = b)
   530	      else
   531	        match tA, tB, a, b with
   532	      | .aline W, .point W', .alinePoly f, .value u =>
   533	          if W = W' then decide (pauliAlinePointCondition P W xA xB f u) else true
   534	      | .point W, .aline W', .value u, .alinePoly f =>
   535	          if W = W' then decide (pauliAlinePointCondition P W xB xA f u) else true
   536	      | .dline W, .point W', .dlinePoly f, .value u =>
   537	          if W = W' then decide (pauliDlinePointCondition P W xA xB f u) else true
   538	      | .point W, .dline W', .value u, .dlinePoly f =>
   539	          if W = W' then decide (pauliDlinePointCondition P W xB xA f u) else true
   540	      | .point W, .pauli W', .value u, .pauliOutcome h =>
   541	          if W = W' then decide (pauliPointPauliCondition P W xA h u) else true
   542	      | .pauli W, .point W', .pauliOutcome h, .value u =>
   543	          if W = W' then decide (pauliPointPauliCondition P W xB h u) else true
   544	      | .pairW W, .pair, .bit β, .pairBits bits =>
   545	          decide (pauliPairCondition P W xA β bits)
   546	      | .pair, .pairW W, .pairBits bits, .bit β =>
   547	          decide (pauliPairCondition P W xB β bits)
   548	      | .point W, .pairW W', .value u, .bit β =>
   549	          if W = W' then decide (pauliPointPairCondition P W xB u β) else true
   550	      | .pairW W, .point W', .bit β, .value u =>
   551	          if W = W' then decide (pauliPointPairCondition P W xA u β) else true
   552	      | .ms (.constraint i), .ms (.var j), .msTriple β, .bit γ =>
   553	          if ∃ k : Fin 3, msConstraintVars i k = j then
   554	            decide (pauliPairGamma P xA = 0 ∨
   555	              msWinPredicate (.constraint i) (.var j) (.triple β) (.bit γ))
   556	          else true
   557	      | .ms (.var j), .ms (.constraint i), .bit γ, .msTriple β =>
   558	          if ∃ k : Fin 3, msConstraintVars i k = j then
   559	            decide (pauliPairGamma P xB = 0 ∨
   560	              msWinPredicate (.var j) (.constraint i) (.bit γ) (.triple β))
   561	          else true
   562	      | .point W, .ms (.var j), .value u, .bit β =>
   563	          decide (pauliPointVariableCondition P W xB j u β)
   564	      | .ms (.var j), .point W, .bit β, .value u =>
   565	          decide (pauliPointVariableCondition P W xA j u β)
   566	        | _, _, _, _ => true
   567	    else false
   568	
   569	/-- The Pauli basis test game.  This is `def:pauli-question-distribution` and
   570	`def:pauli-win-predicate` packaged as the symmetric game of
   571	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-367`, paper origin
   572	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1225`.
   573	-/
   574	noncomputable def pauliBasisTest (P : AdmissibleParams) : Game where
   575	  QuestionA := PauliQuestion P
   576	  QuestionB := PauliQuestion P
   577	  AnswerA := PauliAnswer P
   578	  AnswerB := PauliAnswer P
   579	  μ := pauliQuestionDistribution P
   580	  μ_prob := by sorry
   581	  decide := pauliWinPredicate P
   582	
   583	end
   584	
   585	end MIPStarRE.QPBT

1	import MIPStarRE.Quantum.Measurement
     2	import MIPStarRE.LDT.Basic.Distribution
     3	
     4	/-!
     5	# Games, tensor-product strategies, and value
     6	
     7	This file provides the finite game carrier used by the Pauli basis test.  Pure
     8	states are vectors in `EuclideanSpace`, and POVMs use the project's matrix
     9	`Measurement` structure.
    10	
    11	## References
    12	
    13	The source-facing nodes are `def:game`, `def:povm-conventions`,
    14	`def:tensor-product-strategy`, and `def:tensor-product-value` in
    15	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:47-82` and `8-26`.
    16	The paper origin is `references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:10-57`.
    17	-/
    18	
    19	open scoped BigOperators Matrix ComplexOrder
    20	
    21	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
    22	
    23	open MIPStarRE.LDT
    24	open MIPStarRE.Quantum
    25	
    26	/--
    27	A finite two-player one-round game with a probability distribution on question
    28	pairs and a Boolean decision predicate.  This is `def:game` in
    29	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:51-59`, with paper origin
    30	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:10-24`.
    31	-/
    32	structure Game where
    33	  QuestionA : Type
    34	  QuestionB : Type
    35	  AnswerA : Type
    36	  AnswerB : Type
    37	  [questionAFintype : Fintype QuestionA]
    38	  [questionBFintype : Fintype QuestionB]
    39	  [answerAFintype : Fintype AnswerA]
    40	  [answerBFintype : Fintype AnswerB]
    41	  [questionADecidableEq : DecidableEq QuestionA]
    42	  [questionBDecidableEq : DecidableEq QuestionB]
    43	  [answerADecidableEq : DecidableEq AnswerA]
    44	  [answerBDecidableEq : DecidableEq AnswerB]
    45	  μ : Distribution (QuestionA × QuestionB)
    46	  μ_prob : μ.IsProbability
    47	  decide : QuestionA → QuestionB → AnswerA → AnswerB → Bool
    48	
    49	attribute [instance] Game.questionAFintype Game.questionBFintype
    50	  Game.answerAFintype Game.answerBFintype Game.questionADecidableEq
    51	  Game.questionBDecidableEq Game.answerADecidableEq Game.answerBDecidableEq
    52	
    53	/--
    54	The marginal of a joint POVM obtained by post-processing its answer pair.  This
    55	is the POVM convention of `def:povm-conventions` in
    56	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:8-26`; the post-processing operation
    57	is the already formalized `Measurement.postprocess`, with paper origin
    58	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:26-38`.
    59	-/
    60	noncomputable def marginalLeft {α β d : Type*}
    61	    [Fintype α] [Fintype β] [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq β]
    62	    [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d]
    63	    (M : Measurement (α × β) d) : Measurement α d :=
    64	  M.postprocess Prod.fst
    65	
    66	/-- The right marginal of a joint POVM, obtained using `Prod.snd` in
    67	`def:povm-conventions`, `blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:8-26`,
    68	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:26-38`.
    69	-/
    70	noncomputable def marginalRight {α β d : Type*}
    71	    [Fintype α] [Fintype β] [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq β]
    72	    [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d]
    73	    (M : Measurement (α × β) d) : Measurement β d :=
    74	  M.postprocess Prod.snd
    75	
    76	/-- Projectivity of every effect in a POVM (`def:povm-conventions`, blueprint
    77	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:8-26`; paper origin
    78	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:68-72`). -/
    79	def Measurement.IsProjective {α d : Type*} [Fintype α] [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d]
    80	    (M : Measurement α d) : Prop :=
    81	  ∀ a, IsProj (M.effect a)
    82	
    83	/--
    84	The tensor-product strategy of `def:tensor-product-strategy` in
    85	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:61-69` (paper origin
    86	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:26-38`).
    87	-/
    88	structure Strategy (G : Game) where
    89	  ιA : Type
    90	  ιB : Type
    91	  [ιAFintype : Fintype ιA]
    92	  [ιBFintype : Fintype ιB]
    93	  [ιADecidableEq : DecidableEq ιA]
    94	  [ιBDecidableEq : DecidableEq ιB]
    95	  ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA × ιB)
    96	  ψ_norm : ‖ψ‖ = 1
    97	  A : G.QuestionA → Measurement G.AnswerA ιA
    98	  B : G.QuestionB → Measurement G.AnswerB ιB
    99	
   100	attribute [instance] Strategy.ιAFintype Strategy.ιBFintype
   101	  Strategy.ιADecidableEq Strategy.ιBDecidableEq
   102	
   103	/-- The rectangular tensor placement used in strategy probabilities.  This is
   104	the finite-matrix realization of `def:tensor-product-strategy`, blueprint
   105	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:61-69`; paper origin
   106	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:26-38`.
   107	-/
   108	def heteroKron {ιA ιB : Type*} (A : Op ιA) (B : Op ιB) : Op (ιA × ιB) :=
   109	  Matrix.kronecker A B
   110	
   111	/- The Euclidean linear map is the shared action used by the value and distance
   112	functionals.  Keeping it at the Euclidean-space level avoids accidentally
   113	using the function-space supremum norm of `Matrix.mulVec`. -/
   114	/-- Apply a finite matrix to a Euclidean-space state.  This is the Hilbert-space
   115	action underlying `def:tensor-product-value`, paper
   116	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:219-271`. -/
   117	noncomputable def applyOperatorToState {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
   118	    (M : Op ι) (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι) : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι :=
   119	  Matrix.toEuclideanLin M ψ
   120	
   121	/-- The Born weight of an answer pair for a strategy.  Lean-only support for
   122	`def:tensor-product-value`, blueprint `ch12_qpbt_games.tex:71-82`, paper
   123	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:219-271`. -/
   124	private noncomputable def outcomeWeight {G : Game} (S : Strategy G)
   125	    (x : G.QuestionA) (y : G.QuestionB) (a : G.AnswerA) (b : G.AnswerB) : ℝ :=
   126	  let M : MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op (S.ιA × S.ιB) :=
   127	    heteroKron ((S.A x).effect a) ((S.B y).effect b)
   128	  let acted := applyOperatorToState M S.ψ
   129	  (inner ℂ S.ψ acted).re
   130	
   131	/--
   132	The tensor-product value, expressed as the distribution average of the Born
   133	probabilities.  This is `def:tensor-product-value` in
   134	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:71-82`, with paper origin
   135	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:40-57`.
   136	-/
   137	noncomputable def Strategy.value {G : Game} (S : Strategy G) : ℝ :=
   138	  avgOver G.μ (fun xy =>
   139	    ∑ a : G.AnswerA, ∑ b : G.AnswerB,
   140	      if G.decide xy.1 xy.2 a b then outcomeWeight S xy.1 xy.2 a b else 0)
   141	
   142	/--
   143	The tensor-product game value as a conditional supremum over all finite
   144	strategies.  The `sSup (Set.range ...)` form is the csSup formulation requested
   145	for `def:tensor-product-value`, blueprint
   146	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:71-82`, paper origin
   147	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:40-57`; attainment is
   148	intentionally not asserted here.
   149	-/
   150	noncomputable def Game.value (G : Game) : ℝ :=
   151	  sSup (Set.range (fun S : Strategy G => S.value))
   152	
   153	end MIPStarRE.QPBT

## (d) Statement sketch of `MIPStarRE.QPBT.pauli_soundness`

```lean
/-- Soundness function of the Pauli basis test; argument order (ε, m, d, q)
everywhere, per rem:delta-qld-argument-order. Real rpow throughout. -/
noncomputable def deltaQld (a b ε : ℝ) (m d q : ℕ) : ℝ :=
  a * ((m * d : ℕ) : ℝ) ^ a *
    (ε ^ b + (q : ℝ) ^ (-b) + (2 : ℝ) ^ (-(b * ((m * d : ℕ) : ℝ))))

/-- thm:pauli (qpbt-paper 08_…tex:1426-1447): soundness of the Pauli basis test. -/
theorem pauli_soundness :
    ∃ a b : ℝ, 1 ≤ a ∧ 0 < b ∧ b < 1 ∧
      ∀ (P : AdmissibleParams) [FieldModel P.q] (ε : ℝ), 0 < ε →
        ∀ S : Strategy (pauliBasisTest P), 1 - ε ≤ S.value →
          ∃ (ιA' ιB' : Type) (_ : Fintype ιA') (_ : DecidableEq ιA')
            (_ : Fintype ιB') (_ : DecidableEq ιB')
            (φA : EuclideanSpace ℂ S.ιA →ₗᵢ[ℂ]
                    EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA' × PauliRegister P))
            (φB : EuclideanSpace ℂ S.ιB →ₗᵢ[ℂ]
                    EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιB' × PauliRegister P))
            (aux : EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA' × ιB')), ‖aux‖ = 1 ∧
            -- item 1: ‖φA ⊗ φB ψ − aux ⊗ EPR_q^{⊗M}‖ ≤ δ_qld  (squared distance,
            -- via stateDistSq and deltaQld²; or state with ‖·‖ directly — either
            -- form is acceptable, document the choice)
            ‖isometryTensor φA φB S.ψ - idealState P aux‖
                ≤ deltaQld a b ε P.m P.d P.q ∧
            -- item 2, for both players and both bases, summation over u ∈ F_q^M,
            -- w.r.t. the ideal state; O(·) constants absorbed into a (see (e)8)
            ∀ W : PauliKind,
              (∑ u : PauliRegister P,
                ‖(heteroKron
                    (conjIsometry φA ((S.A (pauliQuestion P W)).effect
                      (PauliAnswer.pauliOutcome u) ...decoded))
                    (1 : Op (ιB' × PauliRegister P))
                  - pauliProjOnA'' P W u).mulVec (idealState P aux)‖ ^ 2)
                ≤ deltaQld a b ε P.m P.d P.q ∧
              (symmetric B-side bound)
```

Supporting definitions in Soundness.lean (all NEW, Lean-only):
`idealState P aux := reindexState prodShuffle (vecTensor aux (eprState (PauliRegister P)))`;
`pauliQuestion P W : (pauliBasisTest P).QuestionA := (PauliType.pauli W, 0)` (the
`(Pauli, W)` question has content `0`, image of the 0-level CL function);
`pauliProjOnA'' P W u : Op ((ιA' × Reg) × (ιB' × Reg))` places `pauliProj W u` on the
`A''` factor, identity elsewhere (and the `B''` analogue). The A-side measurement
outcome family is the sub-family of `S.A` at outcomes `PauliAnswer.pauliOutcome u`
(other constructors carry no mass in the ideal comparison; define the family by
pattern-matching `PauliAnswer → Op` with `0` on the other constructors — this is the
faithful reading of "answer summation over `u ∈ F_q^M`").

## (e) Settled encoding decisions (do not re-derive)

1. **Polynomials — representative convention** (issue #0004, `def:polynomials-degree`):
   polynomial-valued objects are representatives, not function classes. Reuse
   `MIPStarRE.LDT.Preliminaries.polyFunc` where a polynomial *class* is quantified.
   Game *answers* are finite coefficient tuples exactly as printed in the paper
   ("given by its d+1 coefficients"): `Fin (d+1) → K`, resp. `Fin (m*d+1) → K`.
   Do not reuse `LDT.AxisLinePolynomial`/`DiagonalLineAnswer` (the LDT diagonal answer
   is function-encoded and `Parameters`-bundled; a bridge can come later).
   `def:ld-meas`/`PolyMeas` are NOT in this closure — do not build them now.
2. **Distributions — match LDT, not PMF**: the LDT question distributions use
   `MIPStarRE.LDT.Distribution` (Finset-supported, real weights, `Error := ℝ`) with
   `IsProbability`, `avgOver`, `map`, `uniformDistribution`, `uniformOnFinset`
   (`LDT/Basic/Distribution.lean`, `DistributionUniform.lean`; product combinators in
   `DistributionProduct.lean` — verify the exact name before use). All QPBT question
   distributions are `Distribution` values; `PMF` only ever via the existing
   `DistributionPMF` bridge, never in game-facing statements.
3. **Measurements**: use `MIPStarRE.Quantum.Measurement`/`Submeasurement`
   (`Quantum/Measurement.lean`) as the POVM carrier; marginals and the bracket
   notation are `Measurement.postprocess` (already `\leanok` for ch12 `def:bracket`).
   Projectivity via `MIPStarRE.Quantum.IsProj`.
4. **States**: pure states as unit vectors of `EuclideanSpace ℂ ι` (the theorem's
   conclusion needs vector norms, isometries `→ₗᵢ[ℂ]` — reuse
   `Quantum/FiniteHilbert.lean` patterns — and `eprState`). The density-matrix
   `LDT.QuantumState` layer is NOT used in the QPBT games layer.
5. **Field model**: reuse `MIPStarRE.LDT.FieldModel q` (bundled `K ≃ Fin q`). The χ
   map (eq:chi-func) interprets `s : K` as an integer through `FieldModel.equiv`;
   the finite-field trace is the basis-independent `Algebra.trace (ZMod 2) K`
   (= Tr of `Algebra.leftMulMatrix`, i.e. eq:def-trace). The self-dual normal basis
   and `def:binary-representation` are NOT in the statement closure and are deferred
   (see OPEN-6). `canonicalComplement` is defined basis-freely by the pivot
   characterization — `j` is a pivot of `W` iff restricting to coordinates `≤ j`
   increases rank — which agrees with the source's RREF construction by the
   basis-independence noted in `def:canonical-complement` (equivalence proof deferred).
6. **Qudit indexing**: the `M = 2^m` qudits and the vectors `F_q^M` are indexed by
   `Cube m := Fin m → Bool`. Never introduce `Fin (2^m)`; `M` appears only as
   `Fintype.card (Cube m)` in docstrings.
7. **Prose claims inside blueprint definitions become companion lemmas**: CL-level
   assertions ("`L_ALine` is a 2-level CL function"), uniformity of `χ(s)`,
   well-definedness remarks — each a named `sorry` lemma next to the definition, not
   a definitional obligation. Definitions themselves are direct and computable-shaped.
8. **Asymptotic `≈`/O(·) → quantitative functionals**: `def:state-distance` /
   `def:povm-distance` are encoded as explicit real error quantities (`stateDistSq`,
   `opFamilyDistSq`), mirroring how the LDT track already quantifies `≃`/`≈`
   (cf. rem:asymptotic-distance). The implicit universal constants of the blueprint's
   `≈_δ` are absorbed into the existentially quantified constant `a` of
   `pauli_soundness`; record this in the theorem docstring.
9. **Win predicates are `Bool`-valued**, answer alphabets are sum types, and
   "answers not of the prescribed form are rejected" is a predicate clause (match on
   constructor shape). Question alphabets are `Type × ambient-space` pairs — contents
   are full ambient vectors `ι → K` (images of the CL maps), not per-type refined
   types; this matches the blueprint's `(t, L_t(z))` format.
10. **`deltaQld` argument order** is `(ε, m, d, q)` with `0 < b < 1` strict and
    prefactor `a(md)^a` — per rem:delta-qld-argument-order; do not copy the classical
    `δ_ld` shape.

     4	/-!
     5	# Generalized Pauli operators and EPR states
     6	
     7	The definitions here use finite matrix entries and rank-one projectors, so they
     8	are usable by the later game statements without introducing an abstract
     9	operator algebra.  The Fourier/orthogonality identities are retained as named
    10	proof obligations for subsequent stages.
    11	
    12	## References
    13	
    14	The source-facing nodes are `def:lin-reg`, `def:EPR`, `def:generalized-pauli`,
    15	and `lem:pauli-observable-expansion` in
    16	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:494-652`.  The paper origin is
    17	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:908-1161`.
    18	-/
    19	
    20	open scoped BigOperators Matrix ComplexOrder
    21	
    22	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
    23	
    24	open MIPStarRE.Quantum
    25	
    26	variable {K : Type*} [Field K] [Fintype K] [DecidableEq K]
    27	  [Algebra (ZMod 2) K]
    28	
    29	/-- The two generalized Pauli bases used by the test in `def:generalized-pauli`,
    30	blueprint `ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:529-571`, paper origin
    31	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1052-1096`.
    32	-/
    33	inductive PauliKind where
    34	  | X
    35	  | Z
    36	  deriving DecidableEq, Repr, Inhabited, Fintype
    37	
    38	/-- The binary character used for generalized Pauli phases; see
    39	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1052-1081`.
    40	
    41	It is public because the Fourier expansion declarations below expose this
    42	character in their statement types. -/
    43	noncomputable def phaseSign (t : ZMod 2) : ℂ :=
    44	  if t = 0 then 1 else -1
    45	
    46	/--
    47	The shift operator `τ^X(a)`.  Blueprint `def:generalized-pauli`,
    48	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:529-571`; paper origin
    49	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1052-1096`.
    50	-/
    51	noncomputable def tauShift (a : K) : Op K :=
    52	  fun i j => if i = j + a then 1 else 0
    53	
    54	/--
    55	The phase operator `τ^Z(b)`, with the fixed binary trace in the phase.  It is
    56	the second operator of `def:generalized-pauli` (blueprint lines 529-571; paper
    57	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1052-1096`).
    58	-/
    59	noncomputable def tauPhase (b : K) : Op K :=
    60	  fun i j => if i = j then phaseSign (binTrace K (b * j)) else 0
    61	
    62	/-- The single-qudit eigenvector coordinate used in the tensor-product basis;
    63	see `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1126-1161`. -/
    64	private noncomputable def singlePauliVec (W : PauliKind) (e x : K) : ℂ :=
    65	  match W with
    66	  | .Z => if x = e then 1 else 0
    67	  | .X =>
    68	      (Real.sqrt (Fintype.card K : ℝ) : ℂ)⁻¹ * phaseSign (binTrace K (e * x))
    69	
    70	/--
    71	The normalized single/multi-qudit eigenvector for a Pauli basis label.  For an
    72	index type `ι`, the input `e : ι → K` labels the tensor-product basis vector.
    73	This is the vector form of `def:generalized-pauli`, blueprint
    74	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:550-570`, paper origin
    75	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1101-1122`.
    76	-/
    77	noncomputable def pauliVec {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    78	    (W : PauliKind) (e : ι → K) (x : ι → K) : ℂ :=
    79	  ∏ i : ι, singlePauliVec W (e i) (x i)
    80	
    81	/--
    82	The rank-one projector onto `pauliVec W e`.  This is the projective measurement
    83	element `τ^W_e` in `def:generalized-pauli` (blueprint lines 562-570; paper
    84	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1101-1122`).
    85	-/
    86	noncomputable def pauliProj {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    87	    (W : PauliKind) (e : ι → K) : Op (ι → K) :=
    88	  Matrix.vecMulVec (pauliVec W e) (fun x => star (pauliVec W e x))
    89	
    90	/-- A compact operator-valued form of a generalized Pauli observable from
    91	`def:generalized-pauli`, blueprint `ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:529-571`, paper origin
    92	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1052-1096`.
    93	-/
    94	noncomputable def tauObservable {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    95	    (W : PauliKind) (a : ι → K) : Op (ι → K) :=
    96	  fun x y =>
    97	    ∏ i : ι,
    98	      match W with
    99	      | .X => tauShift (a i) (x i) (y i)
   100	      | .Z => tauPhase (a i) (x i) (y i)
   101	
   102	/--
   103	The EPR vector on a finite label space.  Blueprint `def:EPR`,
   104	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:513-523`; paper origin
   105	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:946-955`.
   106	-/
   107	noncomputable def eprState (V : Type*) [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] [Nonempty V] :
   108	    EuclideanSpace ℂ (V × V) :=
   109	  (EuclideanSpace.equiv (V × V) ℂ).symm
   110	    (fun p : V × V =>
   111	      if p.1 = p.2 then (Real.sqrt (Fintype.card V : ℝ) : ℂ)⁻¹ else 0)
   112	
   113	/-- The EPR vector is normalized on a nonempty finite carrier; see
   114	`def:EPR`, `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:946-955`. -/
   115	theorem eprState_norm (V : Type*) [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] [Nonempty V] :
   116	    ‖eprState V‖ = 1 := by
   117	  sorry
   118	
   119	/--
   120	Fourier expansion of a generalized Pauli observable in the Pauli projectors.
   121	This is `lem:pauli-observable-expansion`, equations `eq:pauli-obs-proj` and
   122	`eq:pauli-inversion-0`, in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:638-652`;
   123	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1141-1161`.
   124	Both directions are deliberately left as proof-level obligations in stage 4.1.
   125	-/
   126	theorem tauObservable_eq_sum_pauliProj {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
   127	    (W : PauliKind) (a : ι → K) :
   128	    tauObservable W a =
   129	      ∑ e : ι → K, phaseSign (binTrace K (dotProduct a e)) • pauliProj W e := by
   130	  sorry
   131	
   132	/-- The inverse Fourier expansion of a Pauli projector
   133	(`lem:pauli-observable-expansion`), blueprint
   134	`ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:638-652`, paper origin
   135	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1141-1161`.
   136	-/
   137	theorem pauliProj_eq_avg_tauObservable {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
   138	    (W : PauliKind) (e : ι → K) :
   139	    pauliProj W e =
   140	      (Fintype.card (ι → K) : ℂ)⁻¹ •
   141	        ∑ a : ι → K, phaseSign (binTrace K (dotProduct a e)) • tauObservable W a := by
   142	  sorry
   143	
   144	end MIPStarRE.QPBT

     3	/-!
     4	# Finite-field bases and the fixed binary representation
     5	
     6	The Pauli basis test uses fields of size `2^k` for odd `k`, together with a
     7	chosen self-dual normal basis over `ZMod 2`.  This file records that choice as
     8	data, while exposing Mathlib's basis and algebra-trace APIs for later proofs.

    10	## References
    11

    13	`def:subfield-trace`, and `def:binary-representation` in
    14	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:182-232` and `298-315`.
    15	Their paper origin is `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:433-502,653-728`.
    16	-/

    25	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:662-667`.

    27	def IsAdmissibleSize (q : ℕ) : Prop := ∃ k : ℕ, Odd k ∧ q = 2 ^ k
    28	
    29	/--

    31	elements by `Fin q`.  The algebra structure and stored basis data make explicit
    32	the paper's once-and-for-all self-dual normal-basis convention; they are
    33	deliberately part of the model rather than quantified afresh by the soundness
    34	theorem.  This is the Lean carrier for `def:binary-representation`, blueprint
    35	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:298-315`, paper origin
    36	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:653-728`.

    38	/- The finite-field carrier is specialized to `Type 0`, as are the finite

    45	  /-- The chosen basis dimension is odd, as required for a self-dual normal basis
    46	  over the binary field. -/

    48	  /-- The admissible field-size relation for the chosen basis dimension. -/

    51	  basis : Module.Basis (Fin basisDim) (ZMod 2) K
    52	  /--
    53	  The inherited coding of `K` is the natural binary encoding of the stored
    54	  basis coordinates.  This field records the source's `downsize` convention
    55	  rather than allowing an unrelated permutation of `Fin q`.  It is the
    56	  coordinate clause of `def:binary-representation` in

    59	  -/
    60	  representation_natural :

   117	    [Algebra F K] [Finite ι]
   118	    (b : Module.Basis ι F K) : K ≃ₗ[F] (ι → F) :=
   119	  b.equivFun

   121	/--

   123	`Algebra.leftMulMatrix`.  It is the multiplication table `K_a` in
   124	`def:subfields-kappa` (blueprint lines 196-199; paper
   125	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:481-502`).
   126	-/
   127	noncomputable abbrev multiplicationTable {F K ι : Type*} [CommSemiring F]
   128	    [Semiring K] [Algebra F K] [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
   129	    (b : Module.Basis ι F K) : K →ₐ[F] Matrix ι ι F :=
   130	  Algebra.leftMulMatrix b
   131	
   132	/--
   133	The finite-field trace used by the Pauli phases.  This is a thin wrapper around
   134	Mathlib's basis-independent `Algebra.trace`, matching `def:subfield-trace` and
   135	Equation `eq:def-trace` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:217-232`
   136	(`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:481-502`).
   137	-/
   138	noncomputable abbrev binTrace (K : Type*) [CommRing K] [Algebra (ZMod 2) K] :
   139	    K →ₗ[ZMod 2] ZMod 2 :=
   140	  Algebra.trace (ZMod 2) K
   141	
   142	/-- The trace selected by a fixed model; this is the map denoted `tr` in the
   143	paper's `def:binary-representation`, blueprint `ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:298-315`,
   144	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:653-680`. -/
   145	noncomputable def fixedBinTrace {q : ℕ} (F : FixedFieldModel q) : F.K → ZMod 2 :=
   146	  binTrace F.K
   147	
   148	/--
   149	The matrix-trace presentation of `fixedBinTrace`, a statement-level bridge to
   150	Equation `eq:def-trace`.  It is the trace assertion in `def:subfield-trace`,
   151	blueprint `blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:217-232`, paper origin
   152	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:481-502`.  Mathlib's
   153	`Algebra.trace_eq_matrix_trace` supplies the basis-independent equality.
   154	-/
   155	theorem fixedBinTrace_eq_matrixTrace {q ι : ℕ} (F : FixedFieldModel q)
   156	    (b : Module.Basis (Fin ι) (ZMod 2) F.K) (a : F.K) :
   157	    fixedBinTrace F a = (multiplicationTable b a).trace := by
   158	  exact Algebra.trace_eq_matrix_trace b a

1	import Mathlib.Data.Matrix.Mul
     2	import Mathlib.LinearAlgebra.Dimension.Finrank
     3	import Mathlib.LinearAlgebra.Projection
     4	
     5	/-!
     6	# Subspaces for the Pauli basis test
     7	
     8	This module supplies the register subspaces, dot-product orthogonals, and the
     9	canonical coordinate complement used by the conditionally linear maps.  The
    10	canonical complement is presented through the intrinsic pivot-rank test; the
    11	equivalence with a particular row-reduced-echelon implementation is a later
    12	construction theorem.
    13	
    14	## References
    15	
    16	The statement-level definitions are `def:register-subspace`,
    17	`def:dot-product-orthogonal`, `def:canonical-complement`, and
    18	`def:cl-canonical` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex`;
    19	the paper origin is `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:231-384`.
    20	-/
    21	
    22	open scoped BigOperators
    23	
    24	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
    25	
    26	variable {K ι : Type*} [Field K] [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    27	
    28	/--
    29	`registerSubmodule K S` is the span of the standard coordinate vectors indexed
    30	by `S`.  It is the Lean encoding of `def:register-subspace` from
    31	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:24-29`, whose paper origin is
    32	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:231-239`.
    33	-/
    34	def registerSubmodule (K : Type*) [Field K] (S : Finset ι) : Submodule K (ι → K) :=
    35	  Submodule.span K {v | ∃ i, i ∈ S ∧ v = Pi.single i 1}
    36	
    37	/--
    38	`dotOrthogonal W` consists of vectors whose coordinate dot product with every
    39	member of `W` vanishes.  This is `def:dot-product-orthogonal` in
    40	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:31-42`, with paper origin
    41	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:241-255`.
    42	-/
    43	def dotOrthogonal (W : Submodule K (ι → K)) : Submodule K (ι → K) where
    44	  carrier := {u | ∀ v, v ∈ W → dotProduct u v = 0}
    45	  zero_mem' := by
    46	    intro v hv
    47	    simp [dotProduct]
    48	  add_mem' := by
    49	    intro u v hu hv w hw
    50	    calc
    51	      dotProduct (u + v) w =
    52	          (dotProduct u w) + (dotProduct v w) := by
    53	            change (∑ i, (u i + v i) * w i) =
    54	              (∑ i, u i * w i) + (∑ i, v i * w i)
    55	            simp_rw [add_mul]
    56	            rw [Finset.sum_add_distrib]
    57	      _ = 0 := by rw [hu w hw, hv w hw, add_zero]
    58	  smul_mem' := by
    59	    intro c u hu v hv
    60	    calc
    61	      dotProduct (c • u) v = c * dotProduct u v := by
    62	        simp [dotProduct, smul_eq_mul, mul_assoc, Finset.mul_sum]
    63	      _ = 0 := by rw [hu v hv, mul_zero]
    64	
    65	/-- Restrict a coordinate vector to the first `k` coordinates.  Lean-only rank
    66	infrastructure for `def:canonical-complement`, blueprint
    67	`ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:84-110`, paper `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:231-384`.
    68	-/
    69	private def prefixMap (k n : ℕ) (hk : k ≤ n) :
    70	    (Fin n → K) →ₗ[K] (Fin k → K) :=
    71	  { toFun := fun x i => x ⟨i.1, lt_of_lt_of_le i.2 hk⟩
    72	    map_add' := by
    73	      intro x y
    74	      rfl
    75	    map_smul' := by
    76	      intro c x
    77	      rfl }
    78	
    79	/-- The rank of a prefix restriction used by the pivot characterization. -/
    80	private noncomputable def prefixRank {n : ℕ} (W : Submodule K (Fin n → K))
    81	    (k : ℕ) (hk : k ≤ n) : ℕ :=
    82	  Module.finrank K (W.map (prefixMap k n hk))
    83	
    84	/--
    85	The non-pivot coordinate set of `W`, defined by the rank-increase
    86	characterization of pivots.  This is the basis-free encoding approved for
    87	`def:canonical-complement` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:84-110`;
    88	the paper's Gaussian-elimination presentation is
    89	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:303-320`.
    90	-/
    91	noncomputable def canonicalComplement {n : ℕ}
    92	    (W : Submodule K (Fin n → K)) : Finset (Fin n) :=
    93	  Finset.univ.filter fun j =>
    94	    prefixRank W (j.1 + 1) (Nat.succ_le_of_lt j.2) =
    95	      prefixRank W j.1 j.2.le
    96	
    97	/--
    98	The canonical coordinate complement spans a complement of `W`.  This is the
    99	proposition `lem:canonical-complement` in
   100	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:112-120`, with paper origin
   101	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:342-373`.
   102	The proof is intentionally deferred in the stage-4.1 skeleton.
   103	-/
   104	theorem isCompl_registerSubmodule_canonicalComplement {n : ℕ}
   105	    (W : Submodule K (Fin n → K)) :
   106	    IsCompl W (registerSubmodule K (canonicalComplement W)) := by
   107	  sorry
   108	
   109	/--
   110	The projector onto the canonical coordinate complement along `W`.  This is
   111	`def:cl-canonical` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:133-145`,
   112	originating at `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:375-384`.
   113	-/
   114	noncomputable def canonicalProjOfKernel {n : ℕ}
   115	    (W : Submodule K (Fin n → K)) : (Fin n → K) →ₗ[K] (Fin n → K) := by
   116	  let T := registerSubmodule K (canonicalComplement W)
   117	  let p : (Fin n → K) →ₗ[K] T :=
   118	    Submodule.projectionOnto T W
   119	      (isCompl_registerSubmodule_canonicalComplement W).symm
   120	  exact T.subtype.comp p
   121	
   122	end MIPStarRE.QPBT

1	import MIPStarRE.LDT.Basic.DistributionUniform
     2	
     3	/-!
     4	# Conditionally linear functions and graph distributions
     5	
     6	The question distributions in the Pauli basis test are generated by a finite
     7	graph of types and a shared seed, with each type applying a conditionally linear
     8	map to that seed.  The inductive predicate below records the level structure
     9	needed by later formalization stages.
    10	
    11	## References
    12	
    13	The source-facing nodes are `def:cl-func`, `def:cl-dist`, `lem:cl-concat`, and
    14	`def:graph-distribution` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:441-535`.
    15	The paper origin is `references/qpbt-paper/05_conditionally_linear_functions.tex:35-57`
    16	and `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1010`.
    17	-/
    18	
    19	open scoped BigOperators
    20	
    21	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
    22	
    23	open MIPStarRE.LDT
    24	
    25	variable {K ι : Type*} [Field K] [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    26	
    27	/--
    28	The source definition is recursive in the residual map.  A direct inductive
    29	predicate with that recursive occurrence under a dependent finite-set index is
    30	rejected by Lean's strict-positivity checker.  We therefore expose the same
    31	public predicate through a positive syntax tree (`CondLinearTerm`), together
    32	with its support invariant and evaluation function.  This is a representation
    33	deviation forced by Lean, not an additional mathematical hypothesis.  It encodes
    34	`def:cl-func`, blueprint `blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:441-463`,
    35	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/05_conditionally_linear_functions.tex:35-57`.
    36	-/
    37	inductive CondLinearTerm (K : Type*) [Field K] {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι]
    38	    [DecidableEq ι] : ℕ → Type _ where
    39	  | zero : CondLinearTerm K (ι := ι) 0
    40	  | succ {ell : ℕ}
    41	      (S₁ : Finset ι)
    42	      (L₁ : (ι → K) →ₗ[K] (ι → K))
    43	      (hSupport : ∀ x i, i ∉ S₁ → L₁ x i = 0)
    44	      (rest : (ι → K) → CondLinearTerm K (ι := ι) ell) :
    45	      CondLinearTerm K (ι := ι) (ell + 1)
    46	
    47	/-- Restrict a coordinate vector to a register, zeroing the complementary
    48	coordinates.  This is Lean-only support for the projections in `def:cl-func`,
    49	blueprint `blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:441-463`, paper origin
    50	`references/qpbt-paper/05_conditionally_linear_functions.tex:35-57`.
    51	-/
    52	def coordinateRestriction (S : Finset ι) (x : ι → K) : ι → K :=
    53	  fun i => if i ∈ S then x i else 0
    54	
    55	/-- Evaluation of a conditionally-linear syntax term.  Lean-only support for
    56	`def:cl-func`, blueprint `ch12_qpbt_games.tex:453-463`, paper origin
    57	`references/qpbt-paper/05_conditionally_linear_functions.tex:35-57`.
    58	-/
    59	def CondLinearTerm.eval {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    60	    {K : Type*} [Field K] :
    61	    {ell : ℕ} → CondLinearTerm K (ι := ι) ell → (ι → K) → (ι → K)
    62	  | _, .zero => fun _ => 0
    63	  | _, .succ S₁ L₁ _ rest =>
    64	      fun x =>
    65	        let x₁ := coordinateRestriction S₁ x
    66	        L₁ x₁ + CondLinearTerm.eval (rest (L₁ x₁)) x
    67	
    68	/-- The support invariant for a conditionally-linear syntax term.  This is a
    69	Lean-only companion to `def:cl-func`, blueprint
    70	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:453-463`, paper origin
    71	`references/qpbt-paper/05_conditionally_linear_functions.tex:35-57`.
    72	-/
    73	def CondLinearTerm.supportedOn {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    74	    {K : Type*} [Field K] :
    75	    {ell : ℕ} → CondLinearTerm K (ι := ι) ell → Finset ι → Prop
    76	  | _, .zero, _ => True
    77	  | _, .succ S₁ _ _ rest, S =>
    78	      S₁ ⊆ S ∧ ∀ y, CondLinearTerm.supportedOn (rest y) (S \ S₁)
    79	
    80	/-- The public conditionally-linear predicate.  Its positive syntax-tree
    81	encoding is the Lean representation of `def:cl-func`, blueprint
    82	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:453-463`, paper origin
    83	`references/qpbt-paper/05_conditionally_linear_functions.tex:35-57`.
    84	-/
    85	def IsCondLinearOn (K : Type*) [Field K] {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι]
    86	    [DecidableEq ι] (S : Finset ι) (ell : ℕ)
    87	    (L : (ι → K) → (ι → K)) : Prop :=
    88	  ∃ t : CondLinearTerm K (ι := ι) ell,
    89	    CondLinearTerm.supportedOn t S ∧ CondLinearTerm.eval t = L
    90	
    91	/--
    92	`IsCondLinear` abbreviates the full-coordinate predicate.  Blueprint
    93	`def:cl-func`, `blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:453-463`; paper
    94	`references/qpbt-paper/05_conditionally_linear_functions.tex:35-57`.
    95	-/
    96	def IsCondLinear (ell : ℕ) (L : (ι → K) → (ι → K)) : Prop :=
    97	  IsCondLinearOn K Finset.univ ell L
    98	
    99	/--
   100	The distribution obtained by applying two conditionally linear maps to a common
   101	uniform seed.  This is `def:cl-dist` in
   102	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:467-470`, paper origin
   103	`references/qpbt-paper/05_conditionally_linear_functions.tex:132-138`.
   104	-/
   105	noncomputable def clDistribution [Fintype K] [DecidableEq K]
   106	    (L R : (ι → K) → (ι → K)) :
   107	    Distribution ((ι → K) × (ι → K)) :=
   108	  (uniformDistribution (ι → K)).map (fun z => (L z, R z))
   109	
   110	/-- The direct-sum map used to encode the paper's CL concatenation.  The left
   111	coordinates carry `L`, while the right coordinates carry the family member
   112	`R u v` selected by the left input `u`.  This is Lean-only coordinate
   113	infrastructure for `lem:cl-concat`, blueprint
   114	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:498-505`, paper origin
   115	`references/qpbt-paper/05_conditionally_linear_functions.tex:315-364`.
   116	-/
   117	def condLinearConcat {ιU ιV : Type*} [Fintype ιU] [DecidableEq ιU]
   118	    [Fintype ιV] [DecidableEq ιV] (L : (ιU → K) → (ιU → K))
   119	    (R : (ιU → K) → (ιV → K) → (ιV → K))
   120	    (x : ιU ⊕ ιV → K) : ιU ⊕ ιV → K :=
   121	  let u : ιU → K := fun i => x (.inl i)
   122	  let v : ιV → K := fun j => x (.inr j)
   123	  Sum.elim (L u) (R (L u) v)
   124	
   125	/--
   126	Concatenating an outer and an indexed inner CL map adds their levels.  This is
   127	`lem:cl-concat` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:498-505`, with
   128	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/05_conditionally_linear_functions.tex:315-364`.
   129	The direct-sum coordinate bookkeeping is represented by `condLinearConcat`; the
   130	level proof remains deferred in this skeleton.
   131	-/
   132	theorem IsCondLinearOn.concat {ιU ιV : Type*} [Fintype ιU] [DecidableEq ιU]
   133	    [Fintype ιV] [DecidableEq ιV] {ell k : ℕ}
   134	    {L : (ιU → K) → (ιU → K)}
   135	    {R : (ιU → K) → (ιV → K) → (ιV → K)}
   136	    (hL : IsCondLinearOn K (Finset.univ : Finset ιU) k L)
   137	    (hR : ∀ u : ιU → K, u ∈ Set.range L →
   138	      IsCondLinearOn K (Finset.univ : Finset ιV) ell (R u)) :
   139	    IsCondLinearOn K (Finset.univ : Finset (ιU ⊕ ιV)) (k + ell)
   140	      (condLinearConcat L R) := by
   141	  sorry
   142	
   143	/--
   144	The graph distribution samples an ordered endpoint pair whose unordered edge
   145	`s(a,b)` lies in `E`, including self-loops.  It is the inlined graph sampler of
   146	`def:graph-distribution` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:553-563`;
   147	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:984-1009`.
   148	The underlying graph-distribution definition is
   149	`references/qpbt-paper/07_types.tex:65-82`.
   150	-/
   151	noncomputable def graphDistribution {T : Type*} [Fintype T] [DecidableEq T]
   152	    (E : Finset (Sym2 T)) (_hE : E.Nonempty) : Distribution (T × T) :=
   153	  Distribution.uniformOnFinset
   154	    (Finset.univ.filter fun ab : T × T => Sym2.mk ab.1 ab.2 ∈ E)
   155	
   156	/-- The graph sampler has unit mass whenever its edge set is nonempty. -/
   157	theorem graphDistribution_isProbability {T : Type*} [Fintype T] [DecidableEq T]
   158	    (E : Finset (Sym2 T)) (hE : E.Nonempty) :
   159	    (graphDistribution E hE).IsProbability := by
   160	  sorry
   161

     4	\subsection{Conditionally linear functions and distributions}
     5	\label{sec:cl}
     6	
     7	We first introduce \emph{conditionally linear functions}, which are used to
     8	specify the question distribution for games considered in the paper in a way
     9	that the question distribution can be ``introspected'', as described in
    10	Section~\ref{sec:introspection}.
    11	Intuitively, a conditionally linear function takes as input an element
    12	$x\in V = \F^n$ for some $n\geq 0$, and applies linear maps $L_j$ sequentially
    13	on $x^{V_j}$ where $V_1,V_2,\ldots $ are a sequence of complementary register
    14	subspaces such that both the linear maps $L_j$ and the subspace $V_j$ for
    15	$j \ge 2$ may depend on the values taken by previous linear maps $L_1(x^{V_1})$,
    16	$L_2(x^{V_2})$, etc.
    17	
    18	In the remainder of the section we use $V$ to denote the linear space $\F^n$ for
    19	some integer $n \geq 0$.
    20	For ease of notation we extensively use the subscript range notation.
    21	For example, if $V_1, V_2, \ldots, V_\ell$ are fixed subspaces of $V$ and $k \in
    22	\{1, 2, \ldots, \ell\}$ we write
    23	\begin{equation*}
    24	  V_{<k} = \bigoplus_{j\,:\,1 \le j<k} V_j\;,\quad
    25	  V_{> k} = \bigoplus_{j\,:\, \ell\ge j > k} V_j\;,
    26	\end{equation*}
    27	and it is understood that $V_{\le k}$ and $V_{\ge k}$ are identical to
    28	$V_{<k+1}$ and $V_{>k-1}$, respectively.
    29	Moreover, if $V'$ is a register subspace of $V$, $F: V' \to V'$ is a function,
    30	and $x \in V$, we write $x^F$ to denote $F(x^{V'})$.
    31	For example, in the following definition $x^{L_1}$ is used as shorthand notation
    32	for $L_1(x^{V_1})$.
    33	
    34	
    35	\begin{definition}
    36	  \label{def:cl-func}
    37		Let $V$ be $\F^n$ for some $n\geq 0$.
    38	  For all integers $\ell\geq 0$ the collection of \emph{$\ell$-level
    39	    conditionally linear functions} (implicitly, \emph{on $V$}) is defined
    40	  inductively as follows.
    41	  \begin{enumerate}
    42	  \item There is a single $0$-level conditionally linear function, which is the
    43	    $0$ function on $V$.
    44	
    45	  \item Let $\ell \geq 1$ and suppose the collection of $(\ell-1)$-level
    46	    conditionally linear functions has been defined.
    47	    The collection of $\ell$-level conditionally linear functions on $V$ consists
    48	    of all functions $L$ on $V$ that can be expressed in the following form.
    49	    There exist complementary register subspaces $V_1$ and $V_{>1}$ of $V$, a
    50	    linear function $L_1$ on $V_1$, and for all $v \in L_1(V_1)$, an
    51	    $(\ell-1)$-level conditionally linear function $L_{>1,\, v}$ on $V_{>1}$,
    52	    such that for all $x\in V$,
    53	    \begin{equation*}
    54	      L(x) = x^{L_1} + L_{>1,\, x^{L_1}} (x^{V_{>1}})\;.
    55	    \end{equation*}
    56	  \end{enumerate}
    57	\end{definition}
    58	
    59	The concept of conditionally linear functions is simple even though the
    60	notations seem complicated.
    61	It is best understood using an operational definition illustrated in
    62	\cref{fig:cl-functions}.
    63	We give an example of a $2$-level CL function in \cref{ex:cl-function}.
    64	
    65	\begin{remark}
    66	  \label{rk:level-1-is-linear}
    67	  It follows from the above definition that all $1$-level CL functions are linear.
    68	\end{remark}
    69	
    70	\begin{example}\label{ex:cl-function}
    71	Consider $V = \F_{2}^{3}$. Then the following map
    72	\begin{equation*}
    73	  L:(x_{0}, x_{1}, x_{2})
    74	  \mapsto (0, x_{0}x_{2} + x_{1}x_{2} + x_{0},  x_{2})
    75	\end{equation*}
    76	on $V$ is a $2$-level CL function by choosing $V_{1} = \mathrm{span}\{(0,0,1)\}$, $L_{1}$
    77	the identity function on $V_{1}$, $V_{2} = V_{1}^{\perp}$, and
    78	\begin{equation*}
    79	  L_{2,\, x_{2}}: (x_{0}, x_{1}, 0)
    80	  \mapsto (0, x_{0}x_{2} + x_{1}x_{2} + x_{0}, 0),
    81	\end{equation*}
    82	which is linear for all $x_{2} \in \F_{2}$.
    83	Note that intuitively the function $L$ selects either $x_{0}$ or $x_{1}$ in the
    84	second coordinate conditioning on the value of $x_{2}$.
    85	\end{example}

   653	\subsubsection{Bit string representations}
   654	\label{sec:ff-representations}
   655	
   656	As mentioned at the end of \Cref{sec:tms}, we sometimes treat the
   657	inputs and outputs of Turing machines as representing elements of a finite
   658	field, or a vector space over a finite field.
   659	We discuss some important details about bit representations of finite field
   660	elements and arithmetic over finite fields.
   661	
   662	In the paper we only consider fields $\F_{2^k}$ where $k$ is odd. 
   663	
   664	\begin{definition}\label{def:admissible-size}
   665	  A field size $q$ is called an \emph{admissible} field size if $q=2^k$ for odd
   666	  $k$.
   667	\end{definition}
   668	
   669	Elements of $\F_2$ are naturally represented using bits. 
   670	To represent elements of $\F_{2^k}$ as binary strings we require the
   671	specification of a basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   672	Given a basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ of $\F_{2^k}$, every element $a \in \F_{2^k}$
   673	has a unique expansion $a = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i e_i$ and can be represented as the
   674	$k$-bit string corresponding to $\downsize(a) \in \F_2^k$.
   675	Note that we omitted the subscript $2$ of $\downsize$ as it maps to the linear
   676	space over the prime subfield $\F_2$.
   677	Thus the \emph{binary representation} of $a \in \F_{2^k}$ is defined as the
   678	natural binary representation of $\downsize(a) \in \F_2^k$ (which in turn is the
   679	\emph{$\F_2$-representation of $a$}).
   680	Throughout the paper we freely associate between the binary representation of a
   681	field element $a \in \F_{2^k}$ and its $\F_2$-representation,
   682	although---technically speaking---these are distinct objects.
   683	
   684	Given the representations $\downsize(a), \downsize(b)$ of $a, b \in \F_{2^k}$, to
   685	compute the binary representation of $a+b$ it suffices to compute the addition
   686	bit-wise, modulo $2$.
   687	Computing the multiplication of elements $a, b$ requires the specification of
   688	the multiplication tables $\{K_{e_i} \in \Matrix_k (\F_2)\}_{i=1}^k $ for the
   689	basis $\{e_i\}$.
   690	Given representations $\downsize(a) = (a_i)_{i=1}^k$, $\downsize(b) =
   691	(b_i)_{i=1}^k$ for $a, b \in \F_{2^k}$ respectively, the representation
   692	$\downsize(ab)$ of the product $ab$ is computed as
   693	\begin{equation}
   694	  \label{eq:eq-mult}
   695	  \downsize(ab) = \sum_{i=1}^k \, a_i \, \downsize \bigl( e_i b \bigr) =
   696	  \sum_{i=1}^k \, a_i \bigl( K_{e_i}\, \downsize (b) \bigr)\;.
   697	\end{equation}
   698	Thus, using our representation for field elements, efficiently performing finite
   699	field arithmetic in $\F_{2^k}$ reduces to having access to the multiplication
   700	table of some basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   701	
   702	The following fact provides an efficient deterministic algorithm for computing a
   703	self-dual normal basis for $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ and the corresponding
   704	multiplication tables for any odd $k$.
   705	
   706	\begin{lemma}
   707	  \label{lem:efficient_basis}
   708	  There exists a deterministic algorithm that given an odd integer $k > 0$,
   709	  outputs a self-dual normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ and the
   710	  multiplication tables of the basis in $\poly(k)$ time.
   711	\end{lemma}
   712	
   713	\begin{proof}
   714		The algorithm of Shoup~\cite[Theorem 3.2]{shoup1990new} shows that for prime
   715	  $p$, an irreducible polynomial in $\Fp[X]$ of degree $k$ can be computed in
   716	  time $\poly(p, k)$.
   717	  Then, the algorithm of Lenstra~\cite[Theorem 1.1]{lenstra1991finding} shows
   718	  that given such an irreducible polynomial, the multiplication table of a
   719	  normal basis of $\F_{p^k}$ over $\Fp$ can be computed in $\poly(k,\log p)$
   720	  time.
   721	  Finally, the algorithm of Wang~\cite{wang1989algorithm} shows that for odd $k$
   722	  and a multiplication table $K$ of a normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$, a
   723	  multiplication table $K'$ for a self-dual normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over
   724	  $\F_2$ can be computed in $\poly(k)$ time.
   725	  Putting these three algorithms together yields the claimed statement.
   726	\end{proof}

   172	% Paper labels sec:finite-fields, sec:subfields, sec:ff-representations kept

   178	Let $p$ be a prime and $q = p^k$ a prime power. We write $\F_p$ and $\F_q$ for
   179	the finite fields with $p$ and $q$ elements; $p$ is the characteristic of
   180	$\F_q$, and $\F_p$ is its prime subfield.
   181	
   182	\begin{definition}[Coordinate map and multiplication tables]\label{def:subfields-kappa}
   183		% The source lets k range over all integers; the extension field exists
   184		% only for k >= 1, so that domain condition is made explicit here.
   185		Let $q$ be a prime power and $k \ge 1$ an integer, so that $\F_q$ is a
   186		subfield of $\F_{q^k}$ and $\F_{q^k}$ is a linear space of dimension $k$
   187		over $\F_q$.
   188		Fix a basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$. The bijection
   189		$\kappa_q : \F_{q^k} \to \F_q^k$ associated with this basis is
   190		\[
   191			\kappa_q : a \mapsto (a_i)_{i=1}^k\;, \qquad
   192			\text{where } a = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i e_i\;.
   193		\]
   194		The map $\kappa_q$ is an isomorphism of $\F_q$-vector spaces; in particular
   195		$\kappa_q(a + b) = \kappa_q(a) + \kappa_q(b)$ for all $a, b \in \F_{q^k}$.
   196		Moreover, multiplication by a fixed element corresponds to a linear map:
   197		for every $a \in \F_{q^k}$ there is a matrix $K_a \in \Mat_k(\F_q)$, the
   198		\emph{multiplication table of $a$ with respect to $\{e_i\}$}, such that
   199		$\kappa_q(ab) = K_a\, \kappa_q(b)$ for all $b \in \F_{q^k}$.
   200		The map extends coordinatewise to vectors, matrices, and sets: for
   201		$v = (v_1, \dots, v_n) \in \F_{q^k}^n$ set
   202		$\kappa_q(v) = (\kappa_q(v_i))_{i=1}^n \in \F_q^{kn}$; for
   203		$M = (M_{i,j}) \in \Mat_{m,n}(\F_{q^k})$ let
   204		$\chi_q(M) \in \Mat_{mk,nk}(\F_q)$ be the block matrix whose $(i,j)$-th
   205		block is $K_{M_{i,j}}$; and for a set $S$ of vectors put
   206		$\kappa_q(S) = \{\kappa_q(v) : v \in S\}$. When $q = p$ is the field
   207		characteristic, the subscript is omitted and we write $\kappa$ and $\chi$.
   208	\end{definition}
   209	
   210	\begin{definition}[Admissible field size]\label{def:admissible-size}
   211		A field size $q$ is \emph{admissible} if $q = 2^k$ for an odd integer $k$.
   212	\end{definition}
   213	
   214	Only fields $\F_{2^k}$ with $k$ odd are used in the analysis of the Pauli basis
   215	test.
   216	
   217	\begin{definition}[Trace of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$]\label{def:subfield-trace}
   218		\uses{def:subfields-kappa, def:admissible-size}
   219		The \emph{trace of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$} is the map
   220		% Paper equation label kept on the display it names.
   221		\begin{equation}\label{eq:def-trace}
   222			\tr_{q^k \to q} : a \mapsto \Tr(K_a)
   223		\end{equation}
   224		for $a \in \F_{q^k}$, where $K_a$ is the multiplication table of $a$ with
   225		respect to the basis $\{e_i\}$. The trace is an $\F_q$-linear map from
   226		$\F_{q^k}$ to $\F_q$, and it is independent of the choice of basis, as can
   227		be seen from the equivalent formula
   228		\[
   229			\tr_{q^k \to q}(a) = \sum_{j=0}^{k-1} a^{q^j}\;.
   230		\]
   231		For admissible $q = 2^k$ we use the shorthand $\tr$ for $\tr_{q \to 2}$.
   232	\end{definition}
   233	
   234	\begin{definition}[Dual, self-dual, and normal bases]\label{def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis}
   235		\uses{def:subfield-trace}
   236		A \emph{dual basis} $\{e_1', \dots, e_k'\}$ of a basis
   237		$\{e_1, \dots, e_k\}$ of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$ is a basis such that
   238		$\tr_{q^k \to q}(e^{}_i e'_j) = \delta_{i,j}$ for all
   239		$i, j \in \{1, \dots, k\}$. A \emph{self-dual basis} is one equal to its own
   240		dual. If for some $\alpha \in \F_{q^k}$ the set
   241		$\{\alpha^{q^j}\}_{j=0}^{k-1}$ forms a basis of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$, that
   242		basis is called a \emph{normal basis}. Self-dual and normal bases do not
   243		exist for every field extension, but for $q = 2$ and odd $k$ a self-dual
   244		normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ always exists; \cite{Ji2020MIPStar}
   245		exhibits one through an explicit construction.
   246	\end{definition}
   247	
   248	\begin{lemma}[Coordinate maps of self-dual bases]\label{lem:downsize_field}
   249		\uses{def:subfields-kappa, def:subfield-trace,
   250			def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis, def:dot-product-orthogonal}
   251		Let $q$ be a prime power, $k \ge 1$ an integer, and $\{e_i\}$ a self-dual
   252		basis of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$. The map $\kappa_q$ corresponding to
   253		$\{e_i\}$ satisfies:
   254		\begin{enumerate}
   255			\item for all $x \in \F_{q^k}$,
   256			      $\kappa_q(x) = \bigl(\tr_{q^k \to q}(x e_1), \dots,
   257			      \tr_{q^k \to q}(x e_k)\bigr)$;
   258			\item for all $x, y \in \F_{q^k}$,
   259			      $\tr_{q^k \to q}(xy) = \kappa_q(x) \cdot \kappa_q(y)$;
   260			\item for all $M \in \Mat_{m,n}(\F_{q^k})$ and $v \in \F_{q^k}^n$,
   261			      $\chi_q(M)\, \kappa_q(v) = \kappa_q(Mv)$.
   262		\end{enumerate}
   263		Items 1 and 2 use self-duality; item 3 holds for an arbitrary basis.
   264	\end{lemma}
   265	\begin{proof}
   266		\uses{def:subfields-kappa, def:subfield-trace, def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis}
   267		For item 1, write $x = \sum_i x_i e_i$, multiply both sides by $e_j$, and
   268		take traces: $\tr_{q^k \to q}(x e_j) = \sum_i x_i \tr_{q^k \to q}(e_i e_j)
   269		= x_j$ by self-duality. For item 2, expand
   270		$xy = \sum_{i,j} x_i y_j e_i e_j$ and take traces; self-duality retains
   271		exactly the diagonal terms, giving $\sum_i x_i y_i = \kappa_q(x) \cdot
   272		\kappa_q(y)$. For item 3, the $i$-th block of $\kappa_q(Mv)$ equals
   273		$\sum_j \kappa_q(M_{i,j} v_j) = \sum_j K_{M_{i,j}}\, \kappa_q(v_j)$, which
   274		is the $i$-th block row of $\chi_q(M)$ applied to $\kappa_q(v)$.
   275	\end{proof}
   276	
   277	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:one}
   278		\uses{def:subfields-kappa, def:subfield-trace, def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis}
   279		Let $k$ be an odd integer and $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ a self-dual normal basis of
   280		$\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$. Then $\tr(e_i) = 1$ for all $i$, and the
   281		representation $\kappa(1)$ of the unit $1 \in \F_{2^k}$ is the all-ones
   282		vector in $\F_2^k$.
   283	\end{lemma}
   284	\begin{proof}
   285		\uses{lem:downsize_field}
   286		Normality gives $e_{i+1} = e_i^2$ (indices taken cyclically), and
   287		$\tr(b^2) = \tr(b)$ for every $b \in \F_{2^k}$ because squaring permutes the
   288		terms of $\tr(b) = \sum_{j=0}^{k-1} b^{2^j}$, using $b^{2^k} = b$. Hence all
   289		the values $\tr(e_i)$ coincide. If the common value were $0$, then $\tr$
   290		would vanish identically on $\F_{2^k}$ by linearity; but then item 1 of
   291		Lemma~\ref{lem:downsize_field} would give $\kappa(b) =
   292		(\tr(b e_1), \dots, \tr(b e_k)) = 0$ for every $b$, contradicting the
   293		bijectivity of $\kappa$. Thus $\tr(e_i) = 1$ for all $i$, and item 1 of
   294		Lemma~\ref{lem:downsize_field} gives
   295		$\kappa(1) = (\tr(e_1), \dots, \tr(e_k)) = (1, \dots, 1)$.
   296	\end{proof}

   298	\begin{definition}[Binary representation of field elements]\label{def:binary-representation}
   299		\uses{def:subfields-kappa, def:admissible-size,
   300			def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis}
   301		Let $q = 2^k$ be an admissible field size. For each odd $k$ we fix, once and
   302		for all, a self-dual normal basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ of $\F_{2^k}$ over

   304		$\{K_{e_i}\}_{i=1}^k$ (Definition~\ref{def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis});
   305		the maps $\kappa$ and $\tr$ always refer to this basis. The \emph{binary
   306		representation} of $a \in \F_{2^k}$ is the $k$-bit string
   307		$\kappa(a) \in \F_2^k$, the \emph{$\F_2$-representation of $a$}; the two are
   308		freely identified. Addition of representations is bitwise addition modulo
   309		$2$, and multiplication is determined by the multiplication tables through
   310		\begin{equation}\label{eq:eq-mult}
   311			\kappa(ab) = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i\, \kappa(e_i b)
   312			= \sum_{i=1}^k a_i \bigl(K_{e_i}\, \kappa(b)\bigr)\;,
   313		\end{equation}
   314		where $\kappa(a) = (a_i)_{i=1}^k$.
   315	\end{definition}

   232	  A \emph{register subspace} $S$ of $V$ is a subspace that is the span of a
   233	  subset of the standard basis of $V$.\footnote{The use of the term ``register''
   234	    is meant to create an analogy for how the space of multiple qubits is often
   235	    partitioned into ``registers'' containing a few qubits each.}
   236	  We often represent such a subspace as an indicator vector $u\in \{0,1\}^s$,
   237	  where $s=\dim(V)$, such that if $\{\hat{e}_1,\ldots,\hat{e}_s\}$ is the standard basis of
   238	  $V$ then $S = \text{span}\{\hat{e}_i|\,u_i=1\}$.
   239	\end{definition}
   240	
   241	\begin{definition}
   242	  Let $\hat{E} = \{ \hat{e}_i\}$ be the standard basis of $V = \F^n$.
   243	  For two vectors $u = \sum_{i=1}^n u_i \hat{e}_i$, $v = \sum_{i=1}^n v_i \hat{e}_i$ in $V$,
   244	  define the \emph{dot product}
   245	  \begin{equation*}
   246	    u \cdot v = \sum_{i=1}^n u_i v_i \in \F\;.
   247	  \end{equation*}
   248	  Let $S$ be a subspace of $V$. The \emph{subspace orthogonal to $S$ in $V$} is
   249	  \begin{equation*}
   250	    S^\perp \,=\, \big\{ u \in V : u \cdot v = 0
   251	    \text{ for all }  v \in S \big\}\;.
   252	  \end{equation*}
   253	  Although the notation $S^\perp$ does not explicitly refer to $V$, the ambient
   254	  space will always be clear from context.
   255	\end{definition}
   256	
   257	We note that over finite fields, the notion of orthogonality does not possess
   258	all of the same intuitive properties of orthogonality over fields such as $\R$
   259	or $\C$; for example, a non-zero subspace $S$ may be orthogonal to itself (e.g.\
   260	$\mathrm{span} \{ (1,1) \}$ over $\F_2$).
   261	However, the following remains true over all fields.
   262	
   263	\begin{lemma}
   264	  \label{lem:perp_perp}
   265	  Suppose $S$ is a subspace of $V$. Then $\dim(S) + \dim(S^\perp) =
   266	  \dim(V)$, and 
   267	  \begin{equation*}
   268	    (S^\perp)^\perp = S\;.
   269	  \end{equation*}
   270	\end{lemma}
   271	
   272	\begin{proof}
   273	  The statement about the dimensions follows from the fact that vectors in $S^\perp$ are
   274	  the solution to a feasible linear system of equations with $\dim(S)$ linearly
   275	  independent rows; this implies that the solution space has dimension exactly
   276	  $\dim(V) - \dim(S)$.
   277	  Next, we argue that $S \subseteq (S^\perp)^\perp$.
   278	  Let $u \in S$.
   279	  Since all vectors $v \in S^\perp$ are orthogonal to every vector in $S$,
   280	  in particular $u$, this implies that $u \in (S^\perp)^\perp$.
   281	  By dimension counting, it follows that $(S^\perp)^\perp = S$.
   282	\end{proof}
   283	
   284	\begin{definition}\label{def:complementary}
   285	  Given a linear space $V$, two subspaces $S$ and $T$ of $V$ are said to form a
   286	  pair of \emph{complementary subspaces} of $V$ if
   287	\begin{equation*}
   288	  S \cap T = \{ 0 \}, \quad S + T = V\;.
   289	\end{equation*}
   290	In this case, we write $V = S \oplus T$.
   291	Any $x\in V$ can be written as $x = x^S + x^T$ for $x^S \in S$ and $x^T \in T$
   292	in a unique way.
   293	We refer to $x^S$ (resp.~$x^T$) as the \emph{projection of $x$ onto $S$ parallel
   294	  to $T$} (resp.~\emph{onto $T$ parallel to $S$}).
   295	We call the unique linear map $L: V \to V$ that maps $x \mapsto x^S$ the
   296	\emph{projector onto $S$ parallel to $T$}.
   297	\end{definition}
   298	
   299	A given subspace may have many different complementary subspaces: consider the
   300	example of $S = \mathrm{span}\{(1,1) \}$ in $\F_2^2$.
   301	Different complementary subspaces include $T = \mathrm{span}\{(1,0)\}$ and
   302	$T' = \mathrm{span}\{(0,1)\}$.
   303	It is convenient to define the notion of a \emph{canonical complement} of a
   304	subspace $S$, given a basis for $S$.
   305	
   306	\begin{definition}
   307	  \label{def:canonical-complement}
   308	  Let $E$ be the standard basis of linear space $V = \F^n$.
   309	  Let $F = \{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_m\} \subset V$ be a set of $m$ linearly
   310	  independent vectors in $V$.
   311	  The \emph{canonical complement $F^\perp$ of $F$} is the set of $n-m$ independent
   312	  vectors defined as follows.
   313	  Write $v_i = \sum_{j=1}^n a_{i, j}\, \hat{e}_j$.
   314		Using a canonical algorithm for Gaussian elimination that works over arbitrary
   315	  fields, transform the $m\times n$ matrix $(a_{i, j})$ to reduced row echelon
   316	  form $(b_{i, j})$.
   317	  Let $J$ be the set of $m$ column indices of the leading $1$ entry in each row
   318	  of $(b_{i, j})$.
   319	  The canonical complement is defined as $F^\perp = \{ \hat{e}_j : j \not\in J \}$.
   320	\end{definition}
   321	
   322	
   323	\begin{remark}
   324	We emphasize that the canonical complement $F^\perp$ is a \emph{set} (rather than
   325	a subspace), and it is defined with respect to a \emph{set} of linearly
   326	independent vectors $F$. While there are equivalent ways of defining
   327	a canonical complement of a \emph{subspace} in a basis-independent manner, 
   328	we use this particular definition because it makes it clear that
   329	the canonical complement of a set $F$ is efficiently computable. 
   330	\end{remark}
   331	
   332	\begin{remark}
   333	  Let $\hat{E}$ be the standard basis of $V$.
   334	  Suppose subspace $S$ is a register subspace of $V$ spanned by
   335	  $\hat{E}_0 \subseteq \hat{E}$.
   336	  Then it is not hard to verify that the canonical complement of $\hat{E}_{0}$ is
   337	  $\hat{E}\setminus \hat{E}_0$ and the span of the canonical complement coincides with
   338	  $S^\perp$.
   339	\end{remark}
   340	
   341	
   342	\begin{lemma}
   343	  \label{lem:canonical-complement}
   344	  Let $S$ be the span of linearly independent vectors $F = \{v_1,\ldots,v_m \}
   345	  \subseteq V$ and let $F^\perp$ be the canonical complement of $F$ as defined
   346	  in Definition~\ref{def:canonical-complement}.
   347	  Let $T = \mathrm{span}(F^\perp)$.
   348	  Then
   349	  \begin{equation*}
   350	   \qquad S + T = V\;,  S \cap T = \{ 0 \} \;.
   351	  \end{equation*}
   352	\end{lemma}
   353	
   354	\begin{proof}
   355	To show the first item, we must show that every vector in $V$ can be
   356	written as a sum of an element of $S$ and an element of $T$. To do
   357	this, let $A = (a_{i, j})$ be the $m\times n$ matrix over $\F$ whose
   358	rows are the vectors $v_i$, as in Definition~\ref{def:canonical-complement}.

   360	  form.
   361	  Let $J$ be the set of column indices of the leading 1 entries in

   364	  these rows to the columns in $J$ are still linearly independent and
   365	  span $\F^m$. Thus, for any vector $u \in V$, there is some linear
   366	  combination $v$ of rows of $B$ such that $u$ and $v$ agree
   367	  restricted to the columns in $J$. In other words, there exists $v
   368	  \in S$ such that $u_j = v_j$ for all $j \in J$. Hence, $u = v + w$
   369	  for $w \in T$, where $T$ is the canonical complement.
   370	  This shows $S + T = V$.
   371	  Counting dimensions shows that necessarily $S\cap T =
   372	  \{0\}$.
   373	\end{proof}
   374	
   375	\begin{definition}
   376	  \label{def:cl-canonical}
   377	  Let $F \subseteq V$ be a set of linearly independent vectors.
   378	  Let $F^\perp$ be the canonical complement of $F$.
   379	  Define the \emph{canonical linear map $L \in \End(V)$ with kernel basis $F$}
   380	  as the projector onto $T$ parallel to $S$, where $S = \mathrm{span}(F)$ and $T
   381	  = \mathrm{span}(F^\perp)$.
   382	  When the basis $F$ for $S$ is clear from context, we refer to this map as the
   383	  \emph{canonical linear map with kernel $S$.}
   384	\end{definition}
   385	
   386	\begin{definition}
   387	  \label{def:Lperp}
   388	  Let $L \in \End(V)$ be a linear map, and let $F$ be a basis for

1	\chapter{Algebraic preliminaries for the Pauli basis test}
     2	\label{chap:qpbt-algebra}
     3	
     4	This chapter records the algebraic preliminaries needed for the quantum Pauli
     5	basis test, following the preliminaries of \cite{Ji2020MIPStar}: subspace
     6	machinery over finite fields (which underlies the conditionally linear question
     7	distributions of Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-games}), field extensions, traces, and
     8	self-dual bases, the low-degree code, lines in $\F_q^m$, and the generalized
     9	Pauli observables together with the EPR states they act on. Measurements,
    10	strategies, and consistency relations for nonlocal games are treated in
    11	Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-games}; the test itself is defined in
    12	Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-test}.
    13	
    14	\section{Linear spaces and subspaces}
    15	% Paper label sec:linear-spaces kept for cross-reference fidelity.
    16	\label{sec:linear-spaces}
    17	
    18	Linear spaces are always of the form $V = \F^n$ for a finite field $\F$ and an
    19	integer $n \ge 1$, unless explicitly stated otherwise. We write $\hat{E} =
    20	\{\hat{e}_1, \dots, \hat{e}_n\}$ for the standard basis of $V$, where
    21	$\hat{e}_i$ has a $1$ in the $i$-th coordinate and $0$'s elsewhere, and
    22	$\mathrm{End}(V)$ for the set of linear maps from $V$ to itself.
    23	
    24	\begin{definition}[Register subspace]\label{def:register-subspace}
    25		A \emph{register subspace} $S$ of $V$ is a subspace that is the span of a
    26		subset of the standard basis of $V$. Such a subspace is represented by an
    27		indicator vector $u \in \{0,1\}^s$, where $s = \dim(V)$, via
    28		$S = \mathrm{span}\{\hat{e}_i : u_i = 1\}$.
    29	\end{definition}
    30	
    31	\begin{definition}[Dot product and orthogonal subspace]\label{def:dot-product-orthogonal}
    32		For two vectors $u = \sum_{i=1}^n u_i \hat{e}_i$ and
    33		$v = \sum_{i=1}^n v_i \hat{e}_i$ in $V = \F^n$, the \emph{dot product} is
    34		\[
    35			u \cdot v = \sum_{i=1}^n u_i v_i \in \F\;.
    36		\]
    37		For a subspace $S$ of $V$, the \emph{subspace orthogonal to $S$ in $V$} is
    38		\[
    39			S^\perp = \bigl\{ u \in V : u \cdot v = 0 \text{ for all } v \in S \bigr\}\;.
    40		\]
    41		The notation $S^\perp$ leaves the ambient space $V$ implicit.
    42	\end{definition}
    43	
    44	Over finite fields, orthogonality lacks some of the familiar properties it has
    45	over $\R$ or $\C$; for example, a nonzero subspace may be orthogonal to itself,
    46	as is $\mathrm{span}\{(1,1)\}$ over $\F_2$. The following dimension identity
    47	nevertheless holds over every field.
    48	
    49	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:perp_perp}
    50		\uses{def:dot-product-orthogonal}
    51		Let $S$ be a subspace of $V$. Then $\dim(S) + \dim(S^\perp) = \dim(V)$, and
    52		\[
    53			(S^\perp)^\perp = S\;.
    54		\]
    55	\end{lemma}
    56	\begin{proof}
    57		\uses{def:dot-product-orthogonal}
    58		The elements of $S^\perp$ are the solutions of a feasible linear system whose
    59		coefficient matrix has $\dim(S)$ linearly independent rows, so the solution
    60		space has dimension exactly $\dim(V) - \dim(S)$. Every $u \in S$ is
    61		orthogonal to every element of $S^\perp$, so $S \subseteq (S^\perp)^\perp$.
    62		Applying the dimension identity twice shows that
    63		$\dim\bigl((S^\perp)^\perp\bigr) = \dim(S)$, so the inclusion is an equality.
    64	\end{proof}
    65	
    66	\begin{definition}[Complementary subspaces]\label{def:complementary}
    67		Two subspaces $S$ and $T$ of a linear space $V$ form a pair of
    68		\emph{complementary subspaces} of $V$ if
    69		\[
    70			S \cap T = \{0\}\;, \qquad S + T = V\;.
    71		\]
    72		In this case we write $V = S \oplus T$. Every $x \in V$ can be written
    73		uniquely as $x = x^S + x^T$ with $x^S \in S$ and $x^T \in T$; we call $x^S$
    74		(resp.\ $x^T$) the \emph{projection of $x$ onto $S$ parallel to $T$} (resp.\
    75		onto $T$ parallel to $S$). The unique linear map $L : V \to V$ with
    76		$x \mapsto x^S$ is the \emph{projector onto $S$ parallel to $T$}.
    77	\end{definition}
    78	
    79	A subspace may have many complementary subspaces: in $\F_2^2$, the subspace
    80	$S = \mathrm{span}\{(1,1)\}$ has the distinct complements
    81	$\mathrm{span}\{(1,0)\}$ and $\mathrm{span}\{(0,1)\}$. Given a basis of $S$,
    82	one may nevertheless single out a \emph{canonical} complement.
    83	
    84	\begin{definition}[Canonical complement]\label{def:canonical-complement}
    85		\uses{def:register-subspace}
    86		Let $\hat{E}$ be the standard basis of $V = \F^n$ and let
    87		$F = \{v_1, \dots, v_m\} \subset V$ be a set of $m$ linearly independent
    88		vectors. Write $v_i = \sum_{j=1}^n a_{i,j}\, \hat{e}_j$, and, using a
    89		canonical Gaussian-elimination algorithm valid over arbitrary fields,
    90		transform the $m \times n$ matrix $(a_{i,j})$ to reduced row echelon form
    91		$(b_{i,j})$. Let $J$ be the set of $m$ column indices containing the leading
    92		$1$ entry of each row of $(b_{i,j})$. The \emph{canonical complement of $F$}
    93		is the set of $n - m$ standard basis vectors
    94		\[
    95			F^\perp = \{\hat{e}_j : j \notin J\}\;.
    96		\]
    97		The canonical complement is a \emph{set} of vectors, not a subspace.
    98		% Basis-independence made explicit here: the source defines F^perp through
    99		% a basis but does not assert dependence on it; uniqueness of the reduced
   100		% row echelon form gives dependence on span(F) alone.
   101		Although defined through the basis $F$, it depends only on
   102		$\mathrm{span}(F)$ and the ambient standard basis: two bases of the same
   103		subspace form the rows of row-equivalent matrices, which have the same
   104		reduced row echelon form and hence the same pivot set $J$. The presentation
   105		through Gaussian elimination, adopted by \cite{Ji2020MIPStar}, makes the
   106		canonical complement efficiently computable. If $S$ is a register subspace
   107		spanned by $\hat{E}_0 \subseteq \hat{E}$, then the canonical complement of
   108		$\hat{E}_0$ is $\hat{E} \setminus \hat{E}_0$, and its span coincides with
   109		$S^\perp$.
   110	\end{definition}
   111	
   112	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:canonical-complement}
   113		\uses{def:canonical-complement, def:complementary}
   114		Let $S$ be the span of linearly independent vectors
   115		$F = \{v_1, \dots, v_m\} \subseteq V$, let $F^\perp$ be the canonical
   116		complement of $F$, and let $T = \mathrm{span}(F^\perp)$. Then
   117		\[
   118			S + T = V\;, \qquad S \cap T = \{0\}\;.
   119		\]
   120	\end{lemma}
   121	\begin{proof}
   122		\uses{def:canonical-complement}
   123		Let $A = (a_{i,j})$ be the $m \times n$ matrix whose rows are the $v_i$ and
   124		write $A = UB$ with $U$ invertible and $B$ in reduced row echelon form, so
   125		that the rows of $B$ are linearly independent and span $S$. The restrictions
   126		of the rows of $B$ to the columns in $J$ are still linearly independent and
   127		span $\F^m$, so for every $u \in V$ there is $v \in S$ that agrees with $u$
   128		on the coordinates in $J$. The difference $u - v$ is then supported on the
   129		coordinates outside $J$, that is, $u - v \in T$, which proves $S + T = V$.
   130		Counting dimensions forces $S \cap T = \{0\}$.
   131	\end{proof}
   132	
   133	\begin{definition}[Canonical linear map with prescribed kernel]\label{def:cl-canonical}
   134		\uses{def:canonical-complement, lem:canonical-complement, def:complementary}
   135		Let $F \subseteq V$ be a set of linearly independent vectors and let
   136		$F^\perp$ be its canonical complement. The \emph{canonical linear map
   137		$L \in \mathrm{End}(V)$ with kernel basis $F$} is the projector onto $T$
   138		parallel to $S$, where $S = \mathrm{span}(F)$ and
   139		$T = \mathrm{span}(F^\perp)$; this is well defined by
   140		Lemma~\ref{lem:canonical-complement}. Since the canonical complement
   141		depends only on $\mathrm{span}(F)$
   142		(Definition~\ref{def:canonical-complement}), so does $L$, and we also call
   143		it the \emph{canonical linear map with kernel $S$}. Note that
   144		$\ker(L) = S$.
   145	\end{definition}
   146	
   147	\begin{definition}[The map $L^\perp$]\label{def:Lperp}
   148		\uses{def:cl-canonical, def:dot-product-orthogonal}
   149		Let $L \in \mathrm{End}(V)$ be a linear map and let $F$ be a basis for
   150		$\ker(L)^\perp$. Define $L^\perp : V \to V$ as the canonical linear map with
   151		kernel basis $F$. (By the basis-independence noted in
   152		Definition~\ref{def:canonical-complement}, the map $L^\perp$ depends only
   153		on $\ker(L)$ and not on the chosen basis $F$.)
   154	\end{definition}
   155

     3	/-!
     4	# Lines and canonical representatives
     5	
     6	The classical and Pauli question distributions use affine lines in a finite
     7	coordinate space.  This module keeps the zero-direction case explicit and
     8	provides the canonical projection used for line representatives.
     9	
    10	## References
    11	
    12	The source-facing nodes are `def:line`, `prop:line-equiv`, and
    13	`def:line-representative` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:433-492`.

    17	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT

    40	
    41	/--

    49	/--
    50	The diagonal-direction predicate from `def:line`; a prefix of coordinates may

    52	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:106-124`.
    53	-/

    62	theorem linePoints_eq_of_mem {m : ℕ}

    68	The canonical linear representative map of a line direction.  It projects onto

    80	/-- The canonical representative point `lineRepMap v u`.  Blueprint

    82	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:166-174`.

   270	def pauliEdges : Finset (Sym2 PauliType) :=
   271	  let loops := Finset.univ.image (fun t : PauliType => Sym2.mk t t)
   272	  let lineEdges :=
   273	    (Finset.univ : Finset PauliKind).image (fun W =>
   274	      Sym2.mk (.point W) (.aline W)) ∪
   275	      (Finset.univ : Finset PauliKind).image (fun W =>

   278	        Sym2.mk (.point W) (.pauli W))
   279	  let basisEdges :=
   280	    (Finset.univ : Finset PauliKind).image (fun W =>
   281	      Sym2.mk (.point W) (.pairW W)) ∪
   282	      ({Sym2.mk (.point .X) (.ms (.var ⟨0, by decide⟩)),
   283	        Sym2.mk (.point .Z) (.ms (.var ⟨4, by decide⟩))} : Finset (Sym2 PauliType))
   284	  let pairEdges :=
   285	    (Finset.univ : Finset PauliKind).image (fun W =>
   286	      Sym2.mk (.pairW W) .pair)

   289	      Sym2.mk xy.1 xy.2 ∈ msEdges) |>.image (fun xy =>
   290	        Sym2.mk (.ms xy.1) (.ms xy.2))
